questions.question: FSA’s Second Law of Software Architecture is:
options: How is more important than why, so never document intent.
Why is more important than how.
Diagrams without reasons always age better than written decisions.
Only microservices have a “why”; monoliths never need reasons.
questions.explanation: Why is more important than how

reference.book: Fundamentals of Software Architecture, 2nd Edition by Mark Richards and Neal Ford
reference.excerpt: See “Choreography and Orchestration” for our discussion.) Architecture is broader than just the combination of structural elements, which is why our dimensional definition incorporates principles, characteristics, and so on.

questions.question: Architecture characteristics (“-ilities”) primarily describe:
options: The exact hex color of every button in the design system.
Capabilities and success criteria of the system (what it must support).
Only the marketing slogan on the landing page hero.
The exact list of npm packages pinned in package-lock.json.
questions.explanation: Architecture characteristics… define the capabilities of a system… and the criteria for its success

reference.book: Fundamentals of Software Architecture, 2nd Edition by Mark Richards and Neal Ford
reference.excerpt: support, the logical components to implement its behavior, and finally the architecture decisions justifying it all.

questions.question: Logical components in FSA’s model mainly structure:
options: Only DNS TTL values for the marketing CDN edge nodes.
The behavior of the system: domains, entities, and workflows.
Only the physical rack layout in a single data center.
Only the choice of laptop stickers for the architecture team.
questions.explanation: logical components form the domains, entities, and workflows of the application

reference.book: Fundamentals of Software Architecture, 2nd Edition by Mark Richards and Neal Ford
reference.excerpt: Component-based thinking is seeing the structure of a system as a set of logical components, all interacting to perform certain business functions.

questions.question: An architecture decision example from FSA is:
options: Forbidding Presentation from calling the database directly in a layered system.
Requiring every function name to be exactly twelve characters long.
Banning all automated tests so releases feel more exciting.
Requiring every production log line to use the same timestamp format only.
questions.explanation: only the Business and Services layers… can access the database… restricting the Presentation layer

reference.book: Fundamentals of Software Architecture, 2nd Edition by Mark Richards and Neal Ford
reference.excerpt: Make Architecture Decisions An architect is expected to define the architecture decisions and design principles used to guide technology decisions within the team, within the department, or across the enterprise.

questions.question: Why can’t architects do “one big trade-off jamboree” and freeze defaults forever?
options: Because every situation requires re-evaluating trade-offs in context.
Because trade-offs only exist in textbooks and never in production.
Because cloud vendors legally forbid changing architecture decisions.
Because diagram tools crash if you revisit a decision after a week.
questions.explanation: every situation requires us to re-evaluate all those trade-offs

reference.book: Fundamentals of Software Architecture, 2nd Edition by Mark Richards and Neal Ford
reference.excerpt: But we can’t, because every situation requires us to re-evaluate all those trade-offs.

questions.question: True or false: All architectures are products of their context (cost, ops, tooling of their era).
questions.explanation: All architectures are products of their context—keep that in mind as you read this book

reference.book: Fundamentals of Software Architecture, 2nd Edition by Mark Richards and Neal Ford
reference.excerpt: All architectures are products of their context—keep that in mind as you read this book.

questions.question: Ensuring compliance with architecture decisions means:
options: Never checking whether teams follow constraints after the first slide deck.
Continually verifying teams follow documented decisions and design principles.
Deleting the architecture decision records so nobody can violate them.
Letting every layer call every database to maximize “agility.”.
questions.explanation: Ensuring compliance means continually verifying that the development teams are following the decisions

reference.book: Fundamentals of Software Architecture, 2nd Edition by Mark Richards and Neal Ford
reference.excerpt: Ensuring compliance means continually verifying that the development teams are following the decisions and design principles defined, documented, and communicated by the architect.
